nameStory: Old-field panic grass gets its name from its favorite hangout spots - old agricultural fields that have been abandoned and are slowly returning to nature. The "panic" part comes from the Latin "panicum," an ancient name for millet and other grain grasses, and has nothing to do with feeling anxious! Early botanists used this term for many grass species with similar branching flower clusters.
description: Old-field panic grass is a modest native grass that forms small clumps in disturbed areas across New England. This perennial grass typically grows 1-3 feet tall with narrow, pointed leaves and delicate, branching flower clusters that appear in late spring and early summer. Like other rosette grasses in its genus, it has an unusual two-phase growth pattern - producing a low rosette of leaves in fall that overwinters, then sending up flowering stems the following year. It's one of our less showy native grasses, but an important pioneer species in ecological succession.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms loose clumps 1-3 feet tall with a distinctive two-phase growth - overwinters as a flat rosette of leaves, then produces upright flowering stems in spring

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves 2-6 inches long that feel slightly rough to the touch and have a prominent light-colored midvein running down the center

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Airy, open clusters of tiny purple-tinged or greenish flowers that branch outward like a delicate tree, appearing in late spring to early summer

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small, oval seeds about 1-2mm long that turn from green to brown as they mature, often persisting into fall on the dried flower stalks

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Leaf sheaths and stems feel slightly hairy or fuzzy when you run your fingers along them, distinguishing it from smoother grasses

habitat: Look for old-field panic grass in disturbed soils like abandoned farm fields, forest clearings, roadsides, and prairie restorations throughout New England. It prefers well-drained, often sandy or rocky soils and thrives in areas with full sun to partial shade. This adaptable grass often grows alongside other pioneer species like goldenrod, asters, and other native grasses in areas recovering from human disturbance.

seasonality.spring: Overwintered rosettes begin sending up flowering stems in late spring, with the delicate branching flower clusters becoming visible by May or early June.
seasonality.summer: Flowers bloom and set seed through summer, with the airy seed heads becoming more prominent and turning from green to purplish-brown.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and disperse while new basal rosettes form at ground level, preparing to overwinter for next year's growth cycle.
seasonality.winter: Appears as small, flattened rosettes of narrow leaves pressed close to the ground, often partially hidden under snow or leaf litter.

funFact: Old-field panic grass is like nature's calendar - it literally lives in two different years at once! The leaves you see forming a rosette this fall will be the same leaves that produce next summer's flowers, making this grass a living bridge between seasons.
confusionNotes: With over 20 species of rosette grasses (Dichanthelium) in New England, identification can be tricky even for experts. The key is looking for the combination of the two-phase growth habit, moderately hairy texture, and preference for old fields rather than deep woods - many of its relatives prefer shadier forest habitats.
contextualKnowledge: **Uncertainty note**: Given the extremely low observation count (only 1 recorded) in New England, this species may be very rare in the region, possibly misidentified, or the data may be incomplete. Field identification of Dichanthelium species requires expert knowledge as they are notoriously difficult to distinguish from one another.
compareHints: Old-field panic grass differs from its many Dichanthelium relatives primarily by habitat preference - while species like deertongue prefer shady woodlands, old-field panic grass seeks out sunny, disturbed areas. It's less hairy than hairy rosette-panicgrass but more fuzzy than the smooth-leaved broad-leaved panic grass. The branching pattern of its flower clusters and the timing of its growth phases can help separate it from similar species, though expert botanical knowledge is often needed for definitive identification.

Starved witchgrass is much more delicate and sparse than its relatives like deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass, which have wider leaves and more robust growth.
Among its many witchgrass relatives, forked witchgrass stands out for its distinctly Y-shaped branching pattern.
Among its Dichanthelium relatives, broad-leaved panic grass stands out for having the widest leaves - most other rosette grasses have much narrower, linear blades.

Among its rosette grass relatives, round-fruited rosette-panicgrass is distinguished primarily by its perfectly spherical seeds - most others like hairy rosette-panicgrass or deertongue have oval or egg-shaped seeds.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, hairy rosette-panicgrass stands out for its consistently fuzzy, velvety texture - most others like deertongue feel smooth or slightly rough.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Bosc's witchgrass tends to have broader leaves than Starved Witchgrass or Slim-leaf Witchgrass, but narrower leaves than broad-leaved panic grass.
Among its many rosette grass relatives, Slim-leaf Witchgrass stands out for having the narrowest leaves - most other Dichanthelium species have broader, more oval-shaped leaves.
Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, variable witchgrass tends to be more adaptable to different moisture levels than most.
Among its witchgrass relatives, Small-fruited Witchgrass is distinguished primarily by its exceptionally tiny seeds - much smaller than deertongue or broad-leaved panic grass.
Wright's Rosette Grass differs from its relatives like deertongue and the various witchgrasses by forming more perfectly circular, compact rosettes rather than loose clumps.
Compared to its Dichanthelium relatives, slender panic grass is notably more delicate and fine-textured than broad-leaved panic grass, and lacks the dense hairiness of hairy rosette-panicgrass.
Northern witchgrass is distinguished from its Dichanthelium relatives primarily by its northern range preference and smaller overall size.

Among the many panic grass relatives in New England, velvet panicum stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety texture - most other Dichanthelium species are hairy but not nearly as plush-feeling.
Unlike the more common deertongue with its broad leaves and dense shade tolerance, false bearded panic grass has much narrower leaves and prefers wet, open areas.

Among its many Dichanthelium relatives in New England, Heller's rosette grass stands out for its strong preference for partial shade rather than full sun, and its consistently neat rosette growth pattern.

Among the rosette grasses, Scribner's Panicgrass is distinguished by its relatively narrow rosette leaves compared to broad-leaved panic grass, and its more pointed leaf tips compared to the rounded leaves of deertongue.

Eaton's Witchgrass is distinguished from its many Dichanthelium relatives by subtle differences in leaf width, flower cluster branching patterns, and seed size - characteristics that often require expert identification.
Among its many Dichanthelium relatives, old field panic grass is distinguished by its preference for truly open, disturbed habitats rather than woodland edges.
Among New England's rosette grasses, Lindheimer's panicgrass stands out for its nearly hairless leaves and preference for wetter soils.
Hemlock panic grass differs from its Dichanthelium relatives by its preference for coniferous rather than deciduous woods and its particularly delicate, narrow leaves.
